summary: Piperazine is an anthelmintic used to treat infection with the common roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides) and the threadworm/pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis). It produces a reversible flaccid paralysis of the worm by acting as a GABA-receptor agonist at the helminth neuromuscular junction, hyperpolarising the muscle membrane; the paralysed but living worms then lose their grip on the gut wall and are expelled by normal intestinal peristalsis. For ascariasis it is given as a single oral dose (about 75 mg/kg, up to roughly 3.5-4 g), and for enterobiasis as a 7-day course, with a repeat dose/course after 1-2 weeks for pinworm to deal with reinfection. Piperazine has largely been replaced by benzimidazoles (albendazole, mebendazole) and pyrantel and is no longer marketed in the United States, so dosing follows the BNF, WHO and other national formularies. It is contraindicated in epilepsy and significant renal or hepatic impairment because it can cause neurotoxicity ('worm wobble'), and should be avoided in pregnancy unless necessary.

moa: Piperazine acts directly on the muscle of susceptible nematodes (especially Ascaris and Enterobius) as an agonist at the worm's GABA-gated chloride channels at the neuromuscular junction. By increasing chloride conductance it hyperpolarises the muscle membrane and blocks the response to acetylcholine, producing a reversible flaccid paralysis. The paralysed worms cannot maintain their position against intestinal flow and are expelled alive by normal peristalsis. It does not kill the worms outright and has no significant ovicidal action, which is why a repeat dose is used for pinworm.

preg: Piperazine should be avoided in pregnancy, particularly during the first trimester, unless treatment is clearly necessary; safer alternatives are usually preferred. Use only on specialist advice when essential.
lact: Piperazine is excreted in breast milk in small amounts. It is generally advised to either avoid use or to withhold breastfeeding for about 8 hours after a dose, discarding the expressed milk during that period.
renal: Piperazine is excreted renally and accumulates in renal impairment, increasing the risk of neurotoxicity. It is contraindicated or should be avoided in significant renal impairment.
hepatic: Piperazine should be avoided in hepatic impairment because of the risk of accumulation and neurotoxicity.

No longer marketed in the USA; dosing follows BNF/WHO and other national formularies (single dose for roundworm; 7-day course for threadworm)
Antagonistic with pyrantel/levamisole (spastic vs flaccid paralysis) - never combine

missed: For a single-dose treatment, take the dose when you remember. For a 7-day threadworm course, take a missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; do not double up. Complete the course and any scheduled repeat dose.
overdose: Overdose causes prominent neurotoxicity: muscle incoordination and weakness, ataxia, tremor, nystagmus, vomiting, and in severe cases convulsions and respiratory depression; effects are worse in renal impairment. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive - control seizures with benzodiazepines, support respiration, and consider gastric decontamination if recent ingestion. Piperazine is dialysable, which may help in severe renal impairment.
